report.source_text: Given the progressive nature of his presentation and concern for airway compromise, the patient and provider used shared decision-making to opt to secure the patient’s airway. The patient was intubated using 160 milligrams of ketamine, 80 milligrams of rocuronium, and 7.5 endotracheal tube (ETT) and then was subsequently ventilated and sedated with propofol and ketamine. Initial ventilator settings were lung protective given unclear pathology at this point. Settings included a volume control mode with a tidal volume of 420 ml, positive expiratory end pressure of 5 mmHg, fraction of inspired oxygen of 100%, and peak pressure of 18 mmHg.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 19-year-old previously healthy nonsmoker presented to the ED with acute onset voice change, facial/neck swelling, chest pain, and dyspnea within 2 hours of diving approximately 10-12 feet without breathing equipment. Physical examination revealed palpable crepitus over neck and shoulders, severe edematous oropharynx with tonsillar pillar contact, lip and tongue swelling, and muffled voice, with lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. Chest X-ray demonstrated large volume mediastinal and neck emphysema with concern for possible aspiration in bilateral lower lobes; neck X-ray showed severe subcutaneous emphysema. CT chest revealed fluid filling of bilateral lower lobe bronchi and diffuse interstitial emphysema throughout both lungs, consistent with barotrauma-induced alveolar rupture and increased alveolar pressures. Due to progressive presentation and concern for airway compromise, the patient was intubated using lung-protective ventilation strategy. He was successfully extubated the following day with improving subcutaneous emphysema. Pulmonology consultation recommended outpatient evaluation including pulmonary function tests and diving restriction.
